To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
O2 and antioxidants can affect Ca(2+)+retention by mitochondria, and that these two effects are unrelated to free-radicals and free-radical scavenging.
alpha-tocopherols (and retinol) delay the permeability of the inner membrane to solutes and ions in Ca(2+ )-loaded mitochondria.
the permeability of liver mitochondria to Ca2+ can be modulated by the oxygen tension, the presence of Pi, and the concentration of lipid-soluble antioxidant(s) in the incubation medium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of oxygen in Ca2+ release, and the effect of alpha-tocopheryl succinate and retinol on Ca2+ release and retention in mitochondria.
a new aspect of the antioxidant properties of tocopherol and other lipophilic antioxidants.
the effects of O2, ketone bodies, antioxidants, and other agents on the permeability transition and Ca(2+)/Pi retention capacity of mitochondria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

O2 deprivation, ketone bodies, alpha-tocopherols, and retinol modulate mitochondrial Ca(2+)+ handling by influencing the permeability transition, which in turn may be a key event in the regulation of Ca2+ retention.
the effects of O2, Pi, and antioxidants on mitochondrial Ca(2+), as well as the permeability transition, depend on the metabolic conditions and the experimental system employed.
the permeability-transition phenomenon may be triggered by a variety of stimuli including O2 and Pi, and may be modulated by antioxidants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

alpha-tocopherols and/or retinols are able to delay the Ca2+-releasing permeability transition of mitochondria, thus contributing to Ca(2+)+ homeostasis and to cell protection during O2 deprivation and subsequent reoxygenation.
the mitochondrial permeability transition is a process which is triggered by O2 and/or Pi, and which is modulated by alpha-tocopheryl and retinyl esters.

O2 and Pi may be involved in the initiation of the permeability transition, while antioxidants, including alpha-tocopherols and retinol, may delay the transition, possibly by interfering with the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore.
The main takeaway from our work is that
alpha-tocopherols, in particular alpha-tocopheryl succinate, may protect against mitochondrial Ca(2+), and possibly other, damage by delaying the permeability transition.
mitochondria are able to retain Ca2+ under conditions in which the respiratory chain is not functional.
the permeability of mitochondria to Ca2+ may be affected by O2 and/or antioxidants, which may have implications for the pathogenesis and treatment of ischemia/reperfusion injuries.
